When Children Argue: Help Parents See the Heart Behind the Behavior

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 5:35
Instaread

Few things wear parents down faster than arguing. A parent gives a simple instruction and suddenly finds himself in a courtroom. The child has reasons, objections, explanations, and perhaps a counterproposal. “But I was going to…” “Why do I have to?” “That’s not fair!” “You always make me…” Before long, the parent is arguing too, and what started as a simple instruction has turned into a power struggle.

Church leaders have a tremendous opportunity to help parents see these moments differently. Arguing isn’t simply an annoying behavior to stop. It can reveal something happening in a child’s heart, and that means the argument itself can become an opportunity for discipleship.

Look for Tendencies in the Heart

Jesus makes a profound statement in Matthew 12:34: “For the mouth speaks what the heart is full of.” Words provide a window into the heart. When certain words and responses occur repeatedly, parents can begin looking beyond the individual incident and identify a tendency.

That distinction is important. Parents naturally focus on episodes: “My son argued with me about turning off the video game.” “My daughter became disrespectful when I told her she couldn’t go to her friend’s house.” But heart-based parenting asks another question: What pattern is developing here?

A child who regularly argues when hearing “no” may have difficulty accepting limits. A child who debates every instruction may be struggling with submission to authority. A child who argues whenever corrected may have difficulty receiving feedback. These are bigger than individual behavior problems. They’re tendencies of the heart that need training.

That perspective can bring hope to parents because it changes the goal. Instead of winning the argument, parents can work on developing a new response in the child.

Don’t Take the Bait

Paul’s advice in 2 Timothy 2:23 is remarkably practical for family life: “Don’t have anything to do with foolish and stupid arguments, because you know they produce quarrels.” Children often learn that arguing works. It delays an instruction, keeps a conversation going, wears a parent down, or occasionally changes the answer.

That doesn’t mean parents become cold or refuse to listen to their children. Listening is valuable. Children need appropriate ways to express concerns and disagree respectfully. But there’s a difference between respectful dialogue and arguing. Church leaders can help parents recognize that distinction and teach their children how to communicate disagreement without turning every unwanted decision into a battle.

Replace Arguing with a Better Response

Heart-based parenting isn’t satisfied with telling children what not to do. Children need to know what they should do instead. That’s where training becomes so important.

Parents can identify several predictable places where arguing occurs and practice healthier responses before the next conflict arrives. Three particularly common situations are hearing “no,” receiving an unwanted instruction, and being corrected.
For example, a parent might teach a child to respond to disappointment by saying, “I’m disappointed, but I’ll be okay.” When given an instruction the child doesn’t like, a simple “Okay, Mom” or “Okay, Dad” can become a practiced response. The words themselves aren’t magic. They provide a framework for teaching something deeper: accepting limits, handling disappointment, cooperating with authority, and developing self-control.

Practice is especially powerful because it takes place outside the heat of conflict. Instead of waiting until emotions are high, parents can role-play these situations when everyone is calm. “Let’s practice what you can say when I tell you it’s time to turn off the screen.” “What could you do when I give you an answer you don’t like?” Those short training conversations can gradually establish new patterns in the heart.

Give Parents a Training Plan

One practical way to help families move beyond reactive parenting is to give them a simple four-part strategy: visioning, practicing, correcting, and affirming.

Visioning helps children understand where they’re going: “We’re working on accepting ‘no’ without arguing.” Practicing gives them a chance to develop a better response. Correcting interrupts the old pattern when it appears and redirects the child toward what has been practiced. Affirming recognizes progress: “I know you were disappointed, but you handled that well. That’s maturity.”

Notice how different this is from simply saying, “Stop arguing!” The parent becomes a coach who is intentionally helping a child develop a new pattern.

This is an important message for churches because parents need more than encouragement to “be biblical.” They need practical ways to apply biblical truth on Tuesday afternoon when a ten-year-old refuses to do homework or a teenager wants to debate a decision for the fifteenth time.

The church can equip parents to recognize those ordinary moments as opportunities for spiritual formation. The family becomes a laboratory for developing cooperation, humility, self-control, wisdom, and respect for authority.

Arguing may be the presenting problem, but the goal is much bigger than a quieter house. When parents look for tendencies, they begin to see what Jesus taught—that words reveal what’s happening in the heart. And once parents recognize the heart issue, they can move from repeatedly managing incidents to intentionally training their children for lasting change.

By Dr. Scott Turansky

Dr. Scott Turansky not only designed the Technology Wellness at Home Course, but he’s written 19 books on parenting and the family. He’s also a professor at Concordia University where he teaches the Masters Level Parenting Program. He heads up the National Center for Biblical Parenting and has trained over 500 Biblical Parenting Coaches who work in churches one-on-one with parents. You can learn more at biblicalparenting.org.
